clinicalPearls: A seizure is a transient event caused by abnormal excessive or hypersynchronous neuronal activity; epilepsy is the distinct condition of a chronic underlying tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, so a single or provoked seizure does not by itself constitute epilepsy (though a single seizure with high-risk clinical/EEG features may suffice).
Roughly 5-10% of people experience at least one seizure in life, with peaks in early childhood and late adulthood; epilepsy prevalence is approximately 5-30 per 1000.

The 2017 ILAE scheme classifies seizures by onset as focal, generalized, or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness (intact vs impaired) and motor vs nonmotor onset, replacing the older 'simple/complex partial' and 'secondary generalization' terms.
Focal motor seizures may show a Jacksonian march (spread along the motor strip), and a postictal focal weakness (Todd's paralysis) lasting minutes to hours can mimic a stroke.
Auras are themselves focal seizures with intact awareness; temporal-lobe auras include rising epigastric sensations, foul smells/tastes, fear, deja vu, and micropsia/macropsia.

Typical absence seizures produce brief lapses of consciousness without postural loss or postictal confusion, with a 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave EEG provoked by hyperventilation; they are frequently misdiagnosed as attention-deficit disorder or daydreaming.

Generalized tonic-clonic seizures begin with a tonic phase (ictal cry, apnea/cyanosis, tongue biting, sympathetic surge) evolving to a clonic phase, followed by postictal flaccidity, confusion, headache, and myalgia.

Mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis is the most common cause of focal seizures with impaired awareness and is characteristically medically refractory but responds well to surgery.

Etiology is strongly age-dependent: neonates - perinatal hypoxia-ischemia, infection, and metabolic derangements; young children - febrile seizures; adolescents/young adults - trauma, genetic syndromes, drugs, autoantibodies; older adults - cerebrovascular disease (up to ~50% of new epilepsy over 65), tumor, and degenerative disease.

Distinguishing seizure from syncope: aura, cyanosis, prolonged motor activity (30-60 s), and many minutes to hours of postictal confusion favor seizure, whereas brief loss of consciousness with rapid recovery, pallor, and provocation by pain/standing favor syncope; headache and incontinence are unreliable discriminators.

A transient serum prolactin rise in the first 30 minutes after most generalized and some focal seizures can support a true seizure over a psychogenic event, but is unreliable without a baseline and because some drugs elevate prolactin.
Penetrating head injury carries up to a 45% risk of subsequent epilepsy via epileptogenesis, illustrating how an acquired structural lesion can permanently lower seizure threshold.
harrison.pathophysiology: Seizures arise from a shift in the normal balance between neuronal excitation and inhibition in the CNS. Focal seizure activity begins in a discrete cortical region and can invade surrounding cortex; the hallmark is the electrographic spike produced by near-simultaneous bursting of many excitatory neurons (hypersynchronization). At the cellular level, a prolonged paroxysmal depolarization shift driven by calcium influx opens voltage-dependent sodium channels and generates repetitive action potentials, followed by a GABA- or potassium-channel-mediated hyperpolarizing afterpotential. Spread is normally limited by intact hyperpolarization and feedforward surround inhibition; recruitment of neighboring neurons occurs through rising extracellular potassium, presynaptic calcium accumulation enhancing transmitter release, NMDA-receptor activation, and ephaptic effects, allowing propagation via local and commissural (corpus callosum) pathways. Epilepsy results from a dynamic interplay of endogenous (often genetic, maturational) factors, epileptogenic factors (e.g., severe head trauma, stroke, infection, neurodegeneration, developmental malformations), and precipitating factors (sleep deprivation, stress, hormonal change, toxins, photic stimulation). Many gene mutations affecting ion channels (e.g., SCN1A, KCNQ2), neurotransmitter receptors, and metabolic transporters (e.g., SLC2A1/GLUT-1) underlie specific syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Syncope (vasovagal, cardiac arrhythmia, valvular disease, orthostatic hypotension)
Transient ischemic attack (especially basilar artery TIA)
Metabolic disturbances - hypoglycemia, hypoxia, hyponatremia, hypocalcemia
Sleep disorders - narcolepsy/cataplexy, benign sleep myoclonus
Movement disorders - tics, nonepileptic myoclonus, paroxysmal choreoathetosis
In children: breath-holding spells, night terrors, sleepwalking, benign paroxysmal vertigo, apnea
infectionMimics: CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) - both a cause of acute symptomatic seizures and a mimic via confusion/altered behavior; lumbar puncture is mandatory in HIV-infected patients presenting with a seizure even when asymptomatic
nonInfectiousMimics: Convulsive syncope (brief tonic-clonic-like movements during a faint, especially when kept upright)
Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (side-to-side head movement, ictal eye closure, asynchronous limb shaking, pelvic thrusting, waxing-waning prolonged events)
additionalInvestigations: EEG, including activation procedures (hyperventilation, photic stimulation, sleep, sleep deprivation); a normal routine interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy and is normal in 50-80% of known epilepsy patients on first recording
Prolonged video-EEG telemetry for poorly characterized or refractory events and to distinguish psychogenic from epileptic seizures
MRI (superior to CT) for structural lesions including hippocampal sclerosis and neuronal migration abnormalities; emergent CT when MRI unavailable or mass/infection suspected
Routine bloods - electrolytes, glucose, calcium, magnesium, hepatic and renal function; toxicology screen of blood and urine
Lumbar puncture when meningitis/encephalitis suspected, and mandatory in HIV-infected patients
Serum and CSF autoantibody testing in fulminant epilepsy with psychiatric or cognitive features
Genetic testing in suspected genetic epilepsy syndromes (diagnostic and may guide therapy choice and predict drug toxicity, e.g., HLA-B*1502 and severe cutaneous reactions)
Functional imaging (PET, SPECT) and advanced localization (high-density EEG/ESI, magnetoencephalography/MSI) in medically refractory focal epilepsy
redFlags: Generalized convulsive status epilepticus - continuous or repetitive seizures (practically, GCSE lasting beyond ~5 min); a medical emergency that can cause cardiorespiratory failure, hyperthermia, metabolic derangement, and irreversible CNS injury
After 30-45 minutes of uninterrupted seizures the clinical signs may become subtle while damaging electrographic seizures continue, including in patients paralyzed by neuromuscular blockade
Fulminant new-onset seizures with psychiatric symptoms and cognitive change suggesting autoimmune (e.g., anti-potassium-channel or anti-glutamate-receptor) epilepsy
New seizure in an older adult suggesting cerebrovascular disease, tumor, or degenerative disease
First seizure with focal features, persistent neurologic deficit, fever, or suspected CNS infection prompting urgent imaging and possible lumbar puncture
Atonic 'drop attacks' with high risk of head injury
harrison.prognosis: Outcome varies widely by syndrome and etiology. Typical absence epilepsy and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy generally respond well to medication (though JME remission is uncommon), whereas mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and epilepsies tied to structural lesions or developmental delay are often refractory. About half of patients do not respond to the first medication, and roughly 30% have ongoing seizures despite optimal drug therapy. Favorable predictors for successfully discontinuing therapy include 1-5 years of complete control, a single seizure type (generalized carrying a better prognosis than focal), normal neurologic examination and intelligence, no family history of epilepsy, and a normal EEG; a normal EEG generally implies a better prognosis. People with epilepsy have a death rate roughly 2-3 times that of matched controls, mostly attributable to the underlying cause but also to accidents, status epilepticus, and SUDEP.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish a focal seizure that secondarily generalizes from a primary generalized tonic-clonic seizure because bystanders emphasize the convulsive phase and overlook subtle focal onset/aura - a distinction that materially changes evaluation and treatment.
Misdiagnosing absence epilepsy as attention-deficit disorder or simple daydreaming.
Concluding bizarre paroxysmal stereotyped behavior is non-epileptic; focal (especially frontal-lobe) seizures can produce highly unusual behaviors.
Assuming a normal interictal EEG excludes epilepsy, or that epileptiform discharges by themselves prove epilepsy.
Over-relying on incontinence or headache to separate seizure from syncope, as these are unreliable.
Assuming psychogenic nonepileptic seizures exclude true epilepsy - the two frequently coexist.
Misreading subtle late-stage status epilepticus as resolution when damaging electrographic seizures persist.
harrison.severityClassification: Seizures are classified by ILAE 2017 onset: focal (with intact or impaired awareness, motor or nonmotor), generalized (motor such as tonic-clonic, atonic, myoclonic; or nonmotor/absence), or unknown onset. Severity at the syndromic extreme is status epilepticus: continuous or repetitive seizures with impaired interictal consciousness, subdivided into generalized convulsive status epilepticus (GCSE) and nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE). Although traditionally defined as 15-30 minutes of activity, GCSE is practically treated as an emergency when convulsions last beyond about 5 minutes. Febrile seizures are graded as simple (single, brief, symmetric) versus complex (repeated, lasting over 15 minutes, or with focal features).
